1. **The idea.** The frames show a grid of squares as a pictogram of historical US outcomes. Light squares mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark squares mean the renter was ahead. The label reads "buyer ahead: 73.6% · 87.3%", which looks like a range of shares across scenarios or ranges. The sources named are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. The footer reads "Census vacancy survey: 4.83% a year · 5.59% a year", and there is a "US only · history, not a forecast" caveat. The whole thing is tagged "ILLUSTRATIVE".

2. **What changes.** The dark renter-ahead block in the middle of the grid changes shape from frame to frame. In frames 1–2 it is wider and has a light gap in it. In frames 3 and 6 it is narrower. In frame 5 it is narrower still, and in the lower part it has a notch. The blue marker on the slider at the bottom also moves, sitting at a different position in frames 1, 2 and 3. The "buyer ahead" text appears in frame 3. The "a reference, not Nina's own rent" note appears in frame 4. The slider seems to be a variable being swept, such as rent level or the rate. I can't tell from the image which variable it is.

3. **What it means.** In most of the historical cases shown, the light buyer-ahead squares far outnumber the dark ones. A buyer came out ahead after ten years in roughly 74–87% of cases. Renting won only in a minority, and that minority shrinks or grows as the slider moves. The light squares dominate the grid, but the dark block doesn't disappear.

4. **Advice.** The animation gives no direct instruction. A viewer might infer that buying has usually come out ahead over a ten-year hold, and that the result depends on rent and rates. The on-screen text also warns that this is history, not a forecast, and that the rent shown is a reference rather than the viewer's own.

5. **Source of the suggestion.** The tilt toward buying comes from the on-screen text ("buyer ahead: 73.6% · 87.3%") and the proportion of light squares. The cautions come from the text too: "history, not a forecast", "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "not Nina's own rent". Any advice beyond that, such as "buying is usually better", is my own inference. The animation doesn't tell the viewer to buy or rent.
